title: Attention First
author: Foster, Pete
summary: Pete Foster argues that most classroom-management targets given to new teachers, such as linking to prior learning, asking hands-down questions, or giving precise feedback, are pointless unless the more fundamental skill of securing student attention is in place first, because none of those techniques matter if students aren't actually listening. He identifies three reasons attention gets skipped over in early teacher development: uncertainty about technique, a belief that behaviour will "sort itself out," and a squeamishness about "forcing" attention. The bulk of the post is a granular sequence of techniques for both getting attention, such as a narrated countdown, scanning the room while "being seen looking," and narrating positive compliance, and for giving instructions well: stating task, time, and behaviour explicitly, checking understanding with a hands-down question, pausing and scanning before circulating, and issuing quiet rather than public consequences. He closes with a parallel set of moves for mentors supporting a new teacher, including mid-lesson signalling and modelling the routines outside of lesson time. Throughout, Foster frames attention not as a one-off skill but as a sequence that has to be rebuilt and reinforced at every transition in a lesson.
points: Foster's central claim reframes common early-career teaching targets as downstream of attention: "all the tasks of the teacher will fail if students aren't listening," so attention has to be secured before any other technique can work.
His narrated countdown technique explicitly models both the process and positive compliance in real time, rather than assuming students will infer what's expected from a bare instruction.
He distinguishes "checking instructions are understood" via a hands-down question from simply giving instructions and hoping, treating the check itself as the safeguard against a ragged task start.
His advice to keep behaviour consequences private rather than public is framed as protecting the teacher-student relationship while still holding the line.
quotes: All the tasks of the teacher will fail if students aren’t listening. Too often, new teachers are given targets that take them too quickly beyond the fundamental of ensuring student attention.
Silence in 5… everyone pens down looking this way in 4… thank you, James – already there… 3… absolute silence in 2… waiting on 2 students only now… 1… thank you… zero.
As Doug Lemov would say, be seen looking. Crane your neck and move to a place where you can see.
In narrating the positive, the class see that the norm is following instructions, that the teacher isn’t battling against them.
New teachers often feel they have to get to the content – the actual teaching – but we save time in the long-term if we don’t allow a failure to follow instructions.
